issues.legal_issue: A co-operative society may refuse membership to an applicant who does not satisfy a qualification in its registered bye-laws, and an authority may not compel admission contrary to that qualification when the governing law preserves it.
material_facts: The society’s registered bye-laws limited membership to members of the Parsi community and required committee approval for transfers.
A member sought to transfer his interest to a builder’s association whose proposed transferee did not qualify under the bye-laws.
The society refused the transfer, but the authorities directed it to admit the proposed transferee.
The Court found no provision in the governing legislation or rules that prohibited the society’s membership qualification.
issues.conclusion: The society could insist that the property be dealt with only in accordance with its bye-laws, and the direction to admit the unqualified transferee was set aside.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 24(1) of the Gujarat Co-operative Societies Act, 1961 and Rule 12(2) of the Gujarat Co-operative Societies Rules, 1965, open membership remains subject to qualifications in the Act, rules and bye-laws. Section 30 also regulates transfers of a member’s interest. A member has no independent right to membership apart from the governing statute and bye-laws: Daman Singh v. State of Punjab and State of U.P. v. C.O.D. Chheoki Employees’ Co-operative Society. Damyanti Naranga v. Union of India does not displace those rules for a society governed by co-operative legislation. Bye-laws must be tested against the Act and rules, and the Registrar’s power to direct amendment under Section 14 depends on what is necessary or desirable in the society’s interests.

predicates.appeal_from_membership_direction: A party appealed from an order directing a co-operative society to admit a proposed member.
predicates.registered_bylaw_sets_membership_qualifi: The society had a registered bye-law specifying who could qualify for membership.
predicates.proposed_member_does_not_meet_qualificat: The proposed member did not satisfy the qualification specified in the society’s bye-law.
predicates.governing_law_preserves_bylaw_qualificat: The law governing the society made membership subject to its bye-laws and did not prohibit the qualification.

issues.definition: When an appeal concerns a direction to admit someone who fails a qualification preserved by the governing law, the society may refuse that applicant admission.

issues.legal_issue: A membership qualification in a co-operative society’s bye-laws is not invalidated merely because it distinguishes by religion or community or is challenged as contrary to general constitutional principles or public policy.
material_facts: The society had been formed to provide housing for members of the Parsi community, and its registered bye-laws restricted membership to that community.
A member and a proposed transferee challenged the restriction, relying on public policy and constitutional equality principles.
The Court found that the society was not shown to be an entity subject to fundamental-rights claims as State action and that the governing legislation did not prohibit the restriction.
The member had joined the society subject to its bye-laws.
issues.conclusion: The restriction could not be disregarded or invalidated on the asserted public-policy or constitutional grounds; any policy change of this kind was for the legislature.
issues.legal_principle: Article 19(1)(c) protects the right to form an association, but there is no fundamental right to become a member of a co-operative society. Part III rights are ordinarily enforced against State action, and the society was not shown to be State under Article 12 applying Ajay Hasia. Membership arises from the governing statute, rules, bye-laws and the member’s agreement. Section 23 of the Contract Act addresses unlawful consideration or objects; public policy in the context of a statutory scheme is assessed within that scheme: Renusagar Power Co. Ltd. v. General Electric Co. Public policy is ordinarily governed by established principles and should not be expanded except in clear cases of public harm: Gheru Lal Parakh v. Mahadeodas Maiya. Freedom of contract is itself an important public policy, as explained in Printing and Numerical Registering Co. v. Sampson; public-policy considerations disable rather than enable relief from contractual obligations, as stated in Rodriguez v. Speyer Bros. and Fender v. Mildmay.

predicates.challenge_to_cooperative_membership_byla: A party challenged a co-operative society’s bye-law governing eligibility for membership.
predicates.cooperative_society_not_shown_to_be_stat: The society was not shown to be an entity against which the asserted fundamental rights could be enforced as State action.
predicates.member_voluntarily_accepted_bylaws: A member joined the society subject to its bye-laws.
predicates.governing_law_does_not_prohibit_restrict: The law governing the society did not prohibit the membership restriction.

issues.definition: A challenged membership restriction is not invalidated on general public-policy or constitutional grounds when the society is not shown to be a State actor, the member accepted its bye-laws, and the governing law does not prohibit the restriction.

issues.legal_issue: A voluntary, qualified restriction on transferring an interest in co-operative housing property is not an absolute restraint on alienation merely because it limits transfers to eligible members and requires the society’s consent.
material_facts: The member acquired the property through inheritance and became a member subject to the society’s bye-laws and the governing statutory restrictions.
The bye-laws permitted a transfer to a person qualified for membership, subject to the society’s prior consent.
The restriction was accepted as part of membership and did not prevent every transfer.
issues.conclusion: The transfer restriction was not an absolute restraint on alienation within Section 10 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, and the contrary finding was reversed.
issues.legal_principle: Section 10 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 invalidates a condition absolutely restraining a transferee from parting with an interest in property. It applies to an absolute restraint imposed on a transfer of property, not to a qualified restriction accepted through membership in a co-operative society. Sections 30 and 31 of the Gujarat Co-operative Societies Act regulate transfers and succession to a member’s interest. Partial restraints may be valid, as reflected in Mohammad Raza v. Mt. Abbas Bandi Bibi and Gummanna Shetty v. Nagaveniamma.

predicates.appeal_from_finding_on_transfer_restrict: A party appealed from a finding that a restriction on transferring co-operative housing property was an absolute restraint on alienation.
predicates.property_interest_acquired_subject_to_me: The property interest was acquired through membership in a society and remained subject to its membership terms.
predicates.voluntary_transfer_to_eligible_person_is: A member could voluntarily transfer the interest to an eligible person, subject to the society’s consent.
predicates.restriction_was_voluntarily_accepted: The member accepted the transfer restriction by joining the society or succeeding to the membership interest.

issues.definition: A transfer restriction is not an absolute restraint on alienation when the property interest is held subject to accepted membership terms that permit a voluntary transfer to an eligible person.
